excerpt: Why blind spot collisions happen, who they injure most, and how fault is decided in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: Lane-change crashes number in the hundreds of thousands nationally each year (NHTSA), and blind spot crashes hit motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians hardest. Proper mirror adjustment, shoulder checks, and defensive driving significantly reduce risk. Georgia requires safe, signaled lane changes under O.C.G.A. §§ 40-6-48 and 40-6-123, with a 2-year filing deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina imposes similar duties under S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1900 and 56-5-2150, including a signal for at least the last 100 feet, with a 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Both states apply modified comparative fault rules.

faqs.question: What is a blind spot accident?
faqs.answer: A blind spot accident occurs when a driver fails to see another vehicle, motorcyclist, bicyclist, or pedestrian in an area around their vehicle that is not visible through mirrors or direct line of sight. These crashes most commonly happen during lane changes, merges, and turns.

faqs.question: Who is most at risk for blind spot accidents?
faqs.answer: Motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians face the highest risk because their smaller profiles make them easier to miss. Drivers of compact cars traveling alongside large trucks or SUVs are also at elevated risk due to the larger vehicles' extensive blind zones.

faqs.question: How can I reduce my blind spots while driving?
faqs.answer: Lean your head toward each window and set that side mirror so you can just see your own car — from your normal seat it will then disappear from view — perform shoulder checks before every lane change, use turn signals early, and avoid lingering in other vehicles' blind spots. This is the Blindzone and Glare Elimination (BGE) setting described in a 1995 Society of Automotive Engineers paper. Modern blind spot monitoring systems can supplement but should not replace these habits.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a blind spot accident claim?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines can permanently bar your claim.

faqs.question: Can I recover damages if I was partially at fault for a blind spot accident?
faqs.answer: Yes, both states follow modified comparative fault rules. In Georgia, you can recover if you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, you can recover if you are less than 51% at fault. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault.

faqs.question: What compensation can I receive after a blind spot accident?
faqs.answer: You may recover medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, property damage, and loss of enjoyment of life. When the at-fault driver's conduct was willful, wanton or showed conscious indifference to consequences — proven by clear and convincing evidence — punitive damages may also be available; in Georgia, negligence, even gross negligence, is not enough (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b); Colonial Pipeline Co. v. Brown). Georgia generally caps punitive damages at $250,000 unless the driver intended harm or was impaired by alcohol or drugs; South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, indexed to $739,245 for 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530), with no cap for intentional harm, a related felony conviction, or impairment. If the accident caused a fatality, the family may pursue a wrongful death claim.
